# Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation

Jaeyong Ko^(\*)    Hankyeol Kim^(\*)    Pilsung Kang^(†)
Affiliation: Department of Industrial Engineering, Seoul National
University Affiliation: Seoul, Republic of Korea Affiliation: {jyko22,
hankyeol, pilsung_kang}@snu.ac.kr Affiliation: ^(\*)Equal contribution.
   ^(†)Corresponding author.

###### Abstract

Unified large multimodal models (ULMMs) are able to perform visual
reasoning through interleaved text-image generation, but generating
explicit intermediate images incurs significant computational overhead.
While visual latent reasoning addresses this, most existing methods rely
on vision-language models (VLMs) incapable of visual generation. We
propose Oddin, a novel framework enabling latent visual reasoning in
ULMMs. Oddin replaces intermediate images with compact latent tokens
processed entirely by the understanding branch, reserving the generation
branch for the final output image. We train the model via offline
self-distillation with three objectives, final image generation losses,
text distillation losses, and cross-entropy losses for special tokens.
Oddin surpasses interleaved generation baselines and closed-source VLMs
on average across seven VBVR-Pro visual reasoning tasks. Qualitative
analysis reveals that latent tokens attend to relevant regions in an
input image, demonstrating that ULMMs can perform complex visual
reasoning without generating intermediate images.

## 1 Introduction

Unified large multimodal models (ULMMs) aim to understand and generate
both text and images within a single architecture. Early approaches
adopt a single shared transformer backbone to process both modalities
\[[35](#bib.bib1), [29](#bib.bib2)\]. However, since visual
understanding and generation require distinct capabilities, fully
sharing parameters leads to suboptimal performance \[[26](#bib.bib3),
[2](#bib.bib4)\]. Recent models address this by introducing decoupled
branches for understanding and generation \[[2](#bib.bib4),
[5](#bib.bib5), [4](#bib.bib6)\]. By operating on a shared multimodal
sequence, these models can reason over images and generate new ones
within a single context.

Building on this capability, recent studies apply ULMMs to visual
reasoning through interleaved generation of text and images, showing
that the resulting multimodal interleaved reasoning outperforms
text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) \[[25](#bib.bib31)\] on certain tasks
\[[14](#bib.bib18), [12](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8)\]. However,
generating intermediate images incurs computational overhead, as the
model must reconstruct pixel-level details, including redundant
background regions. In contrast, the information passed between
reasoning steps is far more compact.

Visual latent reasoning addresses this inefficiency by replacing
explicit intermediate images with compact latent representations
\[[31](#bib.bib14), [24](#bib.bib15), [13](#bib.bib13),
[22](#bib.bib11), [6](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib12), [33](#bib.bib17)\].
However, most existing methods are built on vision-language models
(VLMs), which cannot generate images. As a result, they are inapplicable
to visual reasoning tasks requiring visual outputs, such as VBVR-Pro
\[[30](#bib.bib9)\]. ULMMs avoid this limitation, since their generation
branch can produce images. This raises a natural question: can a ULMM
reason with compact latents in place of intermediate images, while still
generating the final visual output?

We propose Oddin,¹¹ 1 Short for “odd interleaved generation,” and a nod
to Odin, the Norse god who sacrificed one eye to gain wisdom. a novel
training framework for latent reasoning in ULMMs. Oddin replaces each
intermediate image with a latent token block processed by the
understanding branch, while the generation branch only produces the
final image. We train Oddin via offline self-distillation, using
reasoning traces generated by the model itself through interleaved
generation. Without explicitly supervising the latent tokens with
intermediate images, we train the latent tokens to implicitly acquire
the required reasoning capabilities at their positions. To achieve this,
we train SenseNova-U1.5 \[[4](#bib.bib6)\] with three losses: a final
image generation loss, a text distillation loss, and a special-token
cross-entropy loss.

Oddin surpasses the performance of interleaved generation and other
baselines. Qualitative analysis reveals that the latent tokens attend to
the specific input regions that the intermediate image was supposed to
draw. These findings show that a unified model can perform visual
reasoning within the understanding branch without relying on
intermediate image generation, while reserving the generation branch for
producing the final image.

## 2 Related work

#### Interleaved Generation for Visual Reasoning.

For visual reasoning, ULMMs can perform interleaved generation,
producing intermediate images within reasoning trace \[[14](#bib.bib18),
[1](#bib.bib19), [12](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8)\]. Most datasets and
benchmarks used in this line of work, such as V\* \[[27](#bib.bib10)\]
and Zebra-CoT \[[12](#bib.bib7)\], target questions with text answers.
Recent ones such as VBVR-Pro \[[30](#bib.bib9)\],
RIG-Bench \[[16](#bib.bib21)\], and GenPuzzle \[[34](#bib.bib22)\]
require the answer itself to be an image. Although intermediate images
do not always help \[[7](#bib.bib20)\], interleaved generation in recent
ULMMs is now strong enough on suitable tasks \[[30](#bib.bib9),
[5](#bib.bib5)\] to serve as a teacher, which Oddin exploits through
self-distillation.

#### Visual Latent Reasoning.

Extending latent reasoning in language models \[[9](#bib.bib23),
[3](#bib.bib24)\], visual latent reasoning replaces explicit
intermediate images with compact latent tokens \[[31](#bib.bib14),
[13](#bib.bib13), [24](#bib.bib15), [23](#bib.bib25),
[15](#bib.bib26)\]. However, these methods are built on VLMs and always
answer in text, so they cannot handle tasks that require image outputs.
In unified models, latent reasoning has mainly been applied to
text-to-image generation \[[18](#bib.bib27), [32](#bib.bib28)\].
LatentUM \[[11](#bib.bib29)\] reasons over visual states in a shared
semantic space, but each state is still a full sequence of generated
visual tokens, and the model requires new pre-training. Oddin adapts a
pretrained ULMM to interleaved latent visual reasoning through offline
self-distillation, replacing each intermediate image with latent tokens.

## 3 Method

![Refer to caption](2610.33062v1/training_overview.png)

Figure 1: (a) Training Overview. The teacher generates interleaved
traces, and the student is trained on the traces where intermediate
images are replaced with latent blocks. (b) Student architecture and
gradient flow. We train the latent token embeddings, latent
block-specific LoRA, and the output embeddings for the \<lnt\> and
\<img\> tokens, while keeping the remaining parameters frozen.

### 3.1 Preliminaries

SenseNova-U1.5 employs a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture using
shared self-attention, with modality-specific branches. The
understanding branch processes multimodal inputs to generate text, and
emitting an \<img\> token triggers the generation branch to produce an
image. During interleaved reasoning, the model alternates between text
and intermediate images $`v_{i}`$ before producing the final answer
image $`a`$. Because the understanding branch controls image generation,
intermediate images can be replaced by other tokens without disrupting
the final image generation.

### 3.2 Interleaved Latent Reasoning of the Unified Model

We aim to replace explicit intermediate images with compact latent
representations that support subsequent reasoning and final-image
generation. To achieve this, we design a latent reasoning mechanism
where the intermediate explicit images $`v_{i}`$ are replaced by latent
blocks $`z_{i}`$. Each latent block $`z_{i}`$ consists of $`K`$
learnable embeddings enclosed by special tokens \<lnt\> and \</lnt\>.

During inference, instead of generating pixel-level images at each
intermediate step, the understanding branch processes these latent
tokens. These tokens help the subsequent reasoning to effectively reach
the final answer $`a`$. The generation branch is used only for
generating a final image $`a`$ when \<img\> is predicted by the
understanding branch. The number of latent blocks and the timing of the
final image are determined by the model.

### 3.3 Offline Self-Distillation

#### Teacher Trace Collection.

We use SenseNova-U1.5 as a teacher model. Given a multimodal query
$`q=(q_{\text{text}},q_{\text{img}})`$, the teacher model generates
interleaved text–image traces for offline self-distillation, as
illustrated in
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Method ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
(a). During this process, we constrain the number of generated images to
match the ground-truth image count. Finally, we use rejection sampling
to keep only the traces whose final image passes the task-specific
scorer.

#### Student Sequence Construction.

As illustrated in the lower part of
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Method ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
(a), we construct the student sequence by replacing each intermediate
image in the teacher trace with a latent block consisting of $`K`$
latent tokens enclosed by \<lnt\> and \</lnt\>, while keeping the
reasoning text unchanged. We retain the final \<img\> token and use the
teacher’s final image as the flow matching target. We also add latent
block usage instructions to the Oddin’s system prompt (See
[Section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Prompts Setting ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")).

### 3.4 Training Objectives

We train the student model using image generation loss, text
distillation loss, and special-token cross-entropy loss, where
$`\lambda`$ denotes the weights and $`T`$ the distillation temperature:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}T^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{CE}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}.
``` |  | (1) |

#### Image generation loss.

We reconstruct the target image $`x`$ from a noisy state
$`x_{t}=tx+(1-t)s\epsilon`$, where $`\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)`$,
$`t\in[0,1]`$, and $`s`$ is the noise scale. Conditioned on the
student’s state $`c_{\theta}`$, the frozen generation branch predicts
the clean image $`\hat{x}_{\theta}=x_{t}+(1-t)v(x_{t},t;c_{\theta})`$.
Inspired by region-focused supervision \[[28](#bib.bib30)\], we
formulate the loss to explicitly penalize errors in edited areas:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon}\left[\operatorname{MSE}(\hat{x}_{\theta},x)+\operatorname{MSE}_{M}(\hat{x}_{\theta},x)\right],
``` |  | (2) |

where $`M`$ is a binary mask indicating the changed regions between the
input and target images. See
[Section A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Image Generation Loss ‣ Appendix A Training Objectives Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
for details.

#### Text distillation loss.

We align the output distributions of the image-conditioned teacher and
the latent-conditioned student through teacher-to-student KL divergence:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{text}}}\operatorname{KL}\left(p_{\mathrm{teacher},i}\,\middle\|\,p_{\mathrm{student},i}\right),
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{text}}`$ contains all aligned
text-prediction positions, excluding predictions of \<lnt\> and \<img\>.
Both distributions use temperature $`T`$ and retain the teacher’s top-50
tokens, with the remaining probability mass aggregated into one tail
probability. See
[Section A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Text Distillation Loss ‣ Appendix A Training Objectives Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
for details.

#### Special-token cross-entropy loss.

At teacher image-generation positions, we supervise \<lnt\> for
intermediate latent blocks and \<img\> for the final image:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}=-\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\pi}\left[\log p_{\mathrm{student},i}(y_{i})\right],
``` |  | (4) |

where $`y_{i}`$ is the target special token and $`\pi`$ balances
intermediate and final events. Probabilities are normalized over the
full vocabulary. See
[Section A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Special-token Cross-Entropy Loss ‣ Appendix A Training Objectives Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
for details.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Method |  Traffic Light |  Separate Object Spinning |  Dot to Dot |  Rotation Puzzle |  Track Object Movement |  Domino Chain |  Sliding Puzzle | Avg. |
| Closed-source VLMs $`+`$ image generation tool |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| GPT-4o $`+`$ GPT-Image-2 | 0.22 | 0.08 | 0.02 | 0.05 | 0.42 | 0.00 | 0.81 | 0.23 |
| GPT-6.1-sol $`+`$ GPT-Image-2 | 0.45 | 0.56 | 0.02 | 0.21 | 0.86 | 0.00 | 0.99 | 0.44 |

### 3.5 Trainable Parameters and Gradient Flow

As shown in
[Figure 1](#S3.F1 "In 3 Method ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")(b),
we train the latent tokens, the special tokens \<lnt\> and \</lnt\>, and
LoRA adapters \[[10](#bib.bib35)\] while freezing all other parameters.
LoRA is active only within latent blocks, including their special
tokens. The image generation and text distillation losses backpropagate
through frozen operations to the latent embeddings and adapters. For the
special-token cross-entropy, we detach the hidden states to update only
the two output embeddings. Initialization and adapter settings are
provided in
[Section A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Trainable Parameters ‣ Appendix A Training Objectives Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation").

## 4 Experiment

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Training Data.

We use seven tasks from VBVR-Pro for which the teacher achieves over
$`20\%`$ success under interleaved reasoning and the final image can be
automatically verified. We train on $`17{,}051`$ successful teacher
traces generated from 7K VBVR-Pro-RL and 21K native-resolution
VBVR-Pro-SFT, using $`1024\times 1024`$ images. Task selection and data
construction are detailed in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Experiment Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation").

#### Evaluation and Baselines.

We evaluate accuracy on $`700`$ held-out problems across seven
VBVR-Pro-RL tasks, with $`100`$ problems per task. We compare our model
against two closed VLMs (GPT-4o \[[19](#bib.bib32)\] and GPT-6.1-sol
\[[20](#bib.bib33)\]) with GPT-Image-2 \[[21](#bib.bib34)\], and three
ULMMs (BAGEL-7B \[[2](#bib.bib4)\], ThinkMorph \[[8](#bib.bib8)\], and
SenseNova-U1.5 \[[4](#bib.bib6)\]). For SenseNova-U1.5, we evaluate two
modes: text CoT and interleaved generation. See
[Section B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
for details.

### 4.2 Result

#### Main results.

Oddin achieves a mean accuracy of $`0.65`$, outperforming all baselines.
The results show two distinct patterns depending on the relative
performance of Interleaved Reasoning and text CoT. On tasks where
Interleaved Reasoning outperforms text CoT (Traffic Light, Separate
Object Spinning, Rotation Puzzle, and Dot to Dot), Oddin further
improves performance without generating intermediate images. The only
exception is Dot to Dot, where Oddin scores 0.14 points lower. On tasks
where Interleaved Reasoning underperforms text CoT (Domino Chain, Track
Object Movement, and Sliding Puzzle), Oddin consistently recovers
performance. It achieves the highest score on Domino Chain, even
surpassing text CoT. Moreover, Oddin reduces token generation by
$`84\%`$ per problem compared to Interleaved Reasoning, replacing an
average of $`7.9`$ images with just one final image and $`4`$ latent
blocks
([Section C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Inference Cost ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")).

![Refer to caption](2610.33062v1/qualitative_analysis.png)

Figure 2: Gaussian smoothed attention of latent blocks on each step in
Dot To Dot task. Values are relative to uniform attention over the image
(1 = evenly spread).

#### Qualitative analysis.

Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Main results. ‣ 4.2 Result ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
visualizes an example of the Gaussian-smoothed attention from each
latent block at a corresponding intermediate step to the input image,
averaged over its 4 latent tokens. In this Dot To Dot task, attention
concentrates around the dot newly connected at that step, following the
drawing order given in the task instruction. This suggests that the
learned latent tokens carry compact, step-specific visual information
aligned with the visual reasoning trace.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose Oddin, a framework that enables ULMMs to
perform visual reasoning using compact latent tokens processed by the
understanding branch. Trained via offline self-distillation, Oddin
learns the visual reasoning capabilities without explicit intermediate
supervision and outperforms baselines on average. Qualitative analysis
shows that the learned latent tokens attend to the relevant regions to
each reasoning step, indicating that ULMMs can perform visual reasoning
within the understanding branch.

#### Limitations and future work.

In some VBVR-Pro tasks, Oddin shows lower performance compared to the
strongest baselines. This indicates that while latent representations
maintain global semantic reasoning, they lack precise spatial
information. Future work will focus on addressing detailed visual
manipulation tasks within the latent space.

## Appendix A Training Objectives Details

This section provides the detailed formulations and implementation
specifics for the three loss components introduced in
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Training Objectives ‣ 3 Method ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation").

### A.1 Image Generation Loss

The target $`x`$ is defined as the final image from a successful teacher
trace. Images are normalized to $`[-1,1]`$. The noisy input is
formulated as $`x_{t}=tx+(1-t)s\epsilon`$, where $`s`$ denotes the noise
scale of the pretrained generation branch. The timestep $`t`$ is
computed as $`t=1-3u/(1+2u)`$ with $`u\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)`$. The
velocity prediction yields the clean-image estimate
$`\hat{x}_{\theta}=x_{t}+(1-t)v(x_{t},t;c_{\theta})`$.

The change mask is constructed by resizing the input image to the target
resolution using bilinear interpolation. A pixel is selected if its
absolute difference from the target exceeds $`0.1`$ in any RGB channel.
A $`9\times 9`$ binary dilation is applied to incorporate neighboring
pixels. Let $`e_{chw}=\hat{x}_{\theta,chw}-x_{chw}`$ denote the
prediction error. The loss terms are defined as:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\operatorname{MSE}(\hat{x}_{\theta},x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{3HW}\sum_{c,h,w}e_{chw}^{2},`$ |  | (5) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\operatorname{MSE}_{M}(\hat{x}_{\theta},x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{c,h,w}M_{hw}e_{chw}^{2}}{\max\left(3\sum_{h,w}M_{hw},1\right)}.`$ |  | (6) |

The masked term averages errors across the selected pixels and RGB
channels, evaluating to zero for empty masks.

### A.2 Text Distillation Loss

Both models process identical reasoning text via teacher forcing. The
teacher receives intermediate images, whereas the student receives
latent blocks. Positions are aligned by text tokens, including text
preceding the first latent block, excluding prediction positions for
\<lnt\> or \<img\>. Teacher distributions are computed without gradients
using the base model and system prompt.

Let $`q_{A,i}`$ denote the full-vocabulary distribution for
$`A\in\{\mathrm{teacher},\mathrm{student}\}`$, and $`K_{i}`$ denote the
teacher’s top-50 tokens. To formulate the KL objective, we define the
aggregated distribution $`p_{A,i}`$ over the modified vocabulary
$`K_{i}\cup\{\text{tail}\}`$ as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{A,i}(w)=\begin{cases}q_{A,i}(w),&\text{if }w\in K_{i},\\
1-\sum_{v\in K_{i}}q_{A,i}(v),&\text{if }w=\text{tail}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (7) |

This formulation extracts 50 token categories and one aggregated tail
category. The teacher-to-student KL divergence is summed across text
positions per trace. The total objective is scaled by a $`T^{2}`$
multiplier.

### A.3 Special-token Cross-Entropy Loss

At positions preceding teacher image-generation events, target tokens
are \<lnt\> for intermediate images and \<img\> for the final image.
Cross-entropy is calculated over the full student vocabulary without
tail aggregation used in
[Section A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Text Distillation Loss ‣ Appendix A Training Objectives Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation").
Within each trace, intermediate \<lnt\> and final \<img\> losses are
averaged independently and weighted equally. Traces lacking intermediate
images optimize only the final \<img\> loss. This weighting schema
defines the parameter $`\pi`$. The preceding hidden states are detached
to restrict gradients strictly to the two special-token output rows.

### A.4 Trainable Parameters

The input embeddings of \<lnt\> and \</lnt\> are initialized from the
pretrained \<img\> and \</img\> embeddings, respectively. Each latent
token embedding is initialized from \<IMG_CONTEXT\>. Latent token
embeddings are independently trainable, and the same ordered set is
reused across all blocks.

LoRA adapters are active exclusively within latent blocks, including
their boundary tokens. The two special-token output rows are initialized
independently from the pretrained \<img\> output row and remain separate
from the input embeddings. The closing token \</lnt\> is inserted after
$`K`$ latent tokens.

All other parameters remain frozen. The image generation and text
distillation losses update the latent embeddings and LoRA adapters. The
text distillation loss additionally updates the two special-token output
rows. The special-token cross-entropy loss updates only these output
rows due to its detached-hidden-state computation.

## Appendix B Experiment Details

### B.1 Hyperparameters

The main configuration uses $`K=4`$ latent tokens per latent block. LoRA
adapters are configured with rank 16 and $`\alpha=32`$. The model is
trained for two epochs with a global batch size of 16. The learning rate
is initialized at $`2\times 10^{-4}`$ and follows a cosine decay
schedule. The loss coefficients are set to
$`\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}=10`$, $`\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.005`$,
$`\lambda_{\mathrm{CE}}=0.1`$, and the temperature is $`T=1.5`$.

### B.2 Training Data

#### Task Selection.

We select tasks from VBVR-Pro using two criteria: (1) the teacher
achieves a task success rate above $`20\%`$ under interleaved reasoning,
ensuring that success traces for self-distillation can be collected and
(2) task success can be automatically verified from the final generated
image. This yields seven tasks: Traffic Light (O-52), Separate Object
Spinning (G-25), Dot to Dot Task (O-34), Rotation Puzzle (O-44), Track
Object Movement (G-8), Domino Chain Branch Path Prediction (O-23), and
Sliding Puzzle (O-47). For brevity, we refer to the Domino Chain Branch
Path Prediction task as Domino Chain.

#### Data Construction.

The VBVR-Pro-RL pool contains $`7{,}000`$ problems across the seven
selected tasks. We hold out $`700`$ problems for evaluation and use the
remaining 6,300 as training candidates, together with 21,000 randomly
sampled VBVR-Pro-SFT problems. VBVR-Pro-SFT input images are rendered
directly at $`1024\times 1024`$ resolution from their rendering
specifications. We retain teacher traces whose final generated image
passes task verification, resulting in 17,051 training traces. Our
grader is adapted from the official VBVR-Pro evaluation code. The image
reconstruction target is the verified teacher-generated final image.

### B.3 Evaluation Details

#### Baselines.

We compare our method against two groups of baselines. First, for
closed-source VLMs, we evaluate gpt-4o and gpt-6.1-sol. Since they
cannot generate images natively, we pair them with GPT-Image-2 to
produce the final image based on their textual reasoning. Second, for
open-weight ULMMs, we evaluate BAGEL-7B, ThinkMorph, and SenseNova-U1.5.
Specifically for SenseNova-U1.5, we compare against two inference modes:
Text CoT, which performs textual reasoning and generates only the final
image, and Interleaved reasoning, which generates explicit intermediate
images alongside text. Our model replaces these intermediate images with
latent blocks while retaining final-image generation.

#### Evaluation configurations.

All open-weight models use greedy text decoding with maximum $`4{,}096`$
new text tokens, $`1024^{2}`$ output resolution, $`50`$ denoising steps,
and text CFG scale $`4.0`$. The remaining sampler settings follow each
model’s official defaults. SenseNova-U1.5 and Oddin use image CFG
$`1.0`$ without CFG renormalization, whereas BAGEL-7B and ThinkMorph use
image CFG $`2.0`$ with CFG renormalization. For closed-source VLMs, we
make one call per problem through the OpenAI Responses API, with the
input frame and the task prompt. The model reasons freely and draws its
answer by calling the GPT-Image-2 image generation tool
($`1024\times 1024`$, medium effort). The number of tool calls is left
to the model, and the maximum output length is $`32{,}000`$ tokens. All
other decoding settings are the API defaults, and denoising steps and
CFG are not controllable.

#### Generation and Answer Selection.

During inference, except BAGEL-7B no method receives the ground-truth
image count. BAGEL-7B is designed to generate one image per call and is
therefore called $`n_{\mathrm{gt}}`$ times. Our model autonomously
selects whether to emit another latent block or generate the final
image, with a maximum of 12 latent blocks. Interleaved Reasoning
generates images without a prescribed count, subject to a maximum of 13
images. We score its last image before \</think\> to exclude images
redrawn in the subsequent answer. If there is no delimiter, we use the
last generated image. For Text CoT and our model, we score the final
generated image.

Figure 3: Masking analysis of latent blocks. Accuracy when latent blocks
are masked from the first block (blue) or from the last block (red).
“all” means masking every block. Black numbers mean identical value.
Bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over 30 problems per task.
The box gives the number of latent blocks per problem.

### B.4 Prompts Setting

#### System prompts.

Each model uses its own system prompt. BAGEL-7B generates one image per
call, so we call it $`n_{\mathrm{gt}}`$ times and feed each generated
image back as context.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Task prompts.

All open-source models receive the original VBVR-Pro task prompt without
modification, as \[image, prompt\]. Since the closed-source VLMs reason
freely on how to solve each task, they receive the same prompt without
its final sentence, which prescribes the number of output images, and
with ”Provide an image showing the final state.” appended.

## Appendix C Additional Analyses

### C.1 Additional Qualitative Analysis

[Figure 4](#A3.F4 "In C.1 Additional Qualitative Analysis ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
shows the latent-block attention on a Domino Chain Branch Path
Prediction problem, visualized as in
[Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In Main results. ‣ 4.2 Result ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation").
As the chain propagates, attention moves along with it, from the
starting dominoes to the two branches. Unlike Dot To Dot, attention
often runs one step ahead, concentrating on the dominoes about to fall
at the next step. This suggests that the latent blocks anticipate the
upcoming state transition rather than only encoding the current one.

![Refer to caption](2610.33062v1/additional_qualitative_analysis.png)

Figure 4: Gaussian-smoothed attention of the latent block at each step
on Domino Chain Branch Path Prediction, shown as in Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Main results. ‣ 4.2 Result ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation").
Attention concentrates around the dominoes that fall at the current and
the next step.

### C.2 Masking Analysis of Latent Blocks

To test whether the latent blocks are used for visual reasoning, we mask
them from the attention at the final image generation step. In
[Figure 3](#A2.F3 "In Generation and Answer Selection. ‣ B.3 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix B Experiment Details ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation"),
both settings mask up to the minimum number of latent blocks present in
each task, while the “all” condition masks every block. Masking every
block lowers accuracy in most tasks and brings it close to zero in
Separate Object Spinning, Dot to Dot, and Sliding Puzzle. Moreover, in
Separate Object Spinning, masking from the last block reduces the
accuracy more than masking from the first, indicating that the final
image generation relies more on the later blocks. In Dot to Dot, the
opposite holds: masking from the first block reduces the accuracy more,
indicating that earlier blocks carry information the later ones cannot
replace. Overall, the latent blocks affect the generation of the final
image, and the blocks that matter differ across tasks.

### C.3 Inference Cost

[Table 2](#A3.T2 "In C.3 Inference Cost ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Oddin: Latent Visual Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models via Self-Distillation from Image Generation")
reports the number of tokens generated per problem, counted separately
for text, latent, and image tokens. Interleaved reasoning generates on
average $`7.9`$ images ($`8{,}135`$ image tokens), whereas Oddin
generates a single final image and about $`4`$ latent blocks ($`24`$
latent tokens), reducing the total number of generated tokens by
$`84\%`$. Oddin also generates $`49\%`$ fewer text tokens than
Interleaved reasoning ($`725\rightarrow 371`$). Its total is close to
that of Text CoT ($`1{,}209`$).

| Method       | Text | Latent        | Image            | Total |
|--------------|------|---------------|------------------|-------|
| Text CoT     | 183  | –             | 1,026 (1 img)    | 1,209 |
| Interleaved  | 725  | –             | 8,135 (7.9 imgs) | 8,860 |
| Oddin (ours) | 371  | 24 (4 blocks) | 1,026 (1 img)    | 1,421 |

Table 2: Average number of generated tokens per problem on the 700
held-out problems. Text tokens include special tokens in the generated
text (e.g., \<think\>). Each $`1024\times 1024`$ image counts as
$`1{,}026`$ tokens ($`1{,}024`$ image tokens plus \<img\> and \</img\>).
A latent block counts as $`6`$ tokens (\<lnt\>, $`K{=}4`$ slots,
\</lnt\>). Input tokens are excluded.
````
